metaDescription: Six larger-format mandolines, from a dial-adjust Gramercy to Mueller and ONCE FOR ALL chopper-style slicers, compared on capacity, stability and cut range.
introParagraphs: With the most room to spend, a mandoline can be a countertop tool rather than a gadget. The Gramercy has a thickness dial and anti-slip feet, the Mueller bundles interchangeable blades with a food container, and two ONCE FOR ALL models enclose their blades in a chopper-style body. Next to them, the OXO and NACOLUS handhelds are the leaner alternatives.

The upgrade over the cheaper handhelds in this series is not razor sharpness. It is infrastructure: a stable base, a container that catches your work, a dial instead of blade swaps, and enough capacity to prep a whole meal in one go. Those features save time in a busy kitchen, but they also take up cabinet space, and some of them add parts to wash.

We evaluated each pick from its listed specs and buyer feedback, scoring capacity, stability, cut range, safety and storage. The sections below explain what a higher cap buys, what it does not, and how to decide between a stand-up slicer, a chopper-style container tool and a plain handheld for the way you actually cook.

products.name: Gramercy 12-Setting Mandoline Slicer Black Edition
products.description:
The Gramercy is the most serious slicer in this lineup. It offers twelve slice settings through a built-in thickness dial, a rotating blade cylinder, a professional 4CR15 stainless steel blade and a non-slip base with anti-slip feet. The listing says you can dial from paper-thin to thick-cut.

The dial changes everything about how it feels to use. Instead of swapping blades or guessing, you turn to the setting you want, and the rotating cylinder switches cutting style without exposing a loose edge. The anti-slip feet then keep the whole frame from creeping across the counter while you work.

The cost is footprint and care. It takes more counter and cabinet space than a handheld, the open blade needs a holder and a respectful hand, and a larger tool has more surfaces to clean. Compared with the OXO, it offers far more control but needs real storage. It is the right pick for anyone who slices several times a week. If you keep it on a shelf and bring it out for gratins, slaws and salad prep, the dial pays for itself in speed alone, and the steady frame makes long sessions less tiring than any handheld.
products.bestFor: Frequent slicers who want dial control and a stable frame.

products.name: Mueller Pro-Series All-in-One Mandoline
products.description:
The Mueller is a prep station more than a slicer. It carries interchangeable blades for dicing, slicing, julienne cuts and grating, plus a container that catches the food and a holder for small items. The listing counts nine blades in its description and twelve in its title, so check what ships in the box.

The container is the quiet hero. Food falls straight into it, which frees counter space and keeps the cutting area tidy. The holder lets you work down to the last piece of onion or pepper without exposing fingers, and with that many blades you can move from dicing for salsa to slicing for gratin on one tool.

More blades mean more parts to store, the blade count is described inconsistently, and the container size is not stated. Against the Gramercy, it chops and dices but offers less dial control for slice thickness. It is the better buy for cooks who dice a lot and want tidy, contained prep. Dry every blade fully before putting it back in the container, and keep the blades together so none is left loose in the sink where a hand could find it.

products.name: ONCE FOR ALL Upgrade Mandoline Slicer Plus
products.description:
The ONCE FOR ALL Plus is the bigger sibling in a chopper-style family. A sharp blade sits hidden in the body, the feeding port is larger than the standard model, and a container collects the food. The listing describes four mode choices and a collapsible design that rinses clean under the tap and folds down for storage.

A bigger port solves the main complaint with enclosed slicers, which is having to cut vegetables into small pieces first. Chunkier onions, peppers and potatoes fit, and the container takes more at once. Because the blade stays hidden, the whole process is gentler on nervous hands.

The slices are less uniform than those from a flat mandoline, and an assembled unit still takes cabinet space even if it folds down. Compared with the Gramercy, thickness control is limited to modes instead of a dial. It suits cooks who want fast chopping and slicing with built-in safety. Expect to push firm vegetables with a steady, even pressure, and to trim round items flat so they sit securely in the port.

products.name: ONCE FOR ALL Safe Mandoline Slicer 4-Mode
products.description:
The standard ONCE FOR ALL is the compact version of the enclosed idea. It has a hidden sharp blade, four modes covering julienne, matchstick, slicing and dicing, and 420 stainless steel blades. The listing says you get all four without changing a blade.

Its virtue is simplicity. You pick a mode, load the port and push, with no blade handling at any point. That makes it a comfortable tool for anyone wary of exposed edges, and the simple design is quick to set up and clean.

Food must be pre-cut to fit the port, and the listing does not state a thickness range for the slicing mode. Compared with the Plus model it has a smaller opening, so it is best for small and medium vegetables. Choose it if you want enclosed safety and a lower learning curve than the dial-based Gramercy. It also suits shared kitchens where several people of different skill levels will reach for the same slicer without reading instructions.

products.name: OXO Good Grips Handheld Mandoline with Non-Slip Handle
products.description:
The OXO remains the sensible handheld in a lineup that leans large. Its three thicknesses of 1, 2.5 and 4 mm cover everyday slicing, a large non-slip handle sits comfortably in the palm, and a stable foot holds it steady. A hook lets it rest on a bowl to catch slices.

At this tier it works as a counterpoint to the bigger tools. It stores flat in a drawer, requires no assembly and asks almost nothing of your counter. Many households find three thicknesses are all they ever use, which makes the Gramercy's twelve settings a luxury rather than a need.

The listing mentions no hand guard, and it lacks julienne or dicing. Against the Mueller, it is far simpler and much more limited. Choose it if the larger picks sound like overkill and a trusted handheld fits your weekly slicing. It is the one pick here you can buy on impulse and still keep using a year later, because there is so little to go wrong.

products.name: NACOLUS 5-in-1 Handheld Mandoline Slicer
products.description:
The NACOLUS gives a handheld five interchangeable blades. The listing names a 3 mm straight slicer, a 2 mm shredder and a waffle cut, with all options built in so there is nothing to fold or assemble. It is designed for quick slicing, grating and shredding.

Five blades go a long way toward the versatility of the Mueller at a fraction of the bulk. You can switch from slicing cucumbers to shredding carrots to cutting waffle fries, all on a compact frame that fits a drawer. The simple structure keeps setup short.

Blade swaps still involve handling edges, and the listing publishes few measurements beyond the named sizes. Beside the Gramercy it lacks a dial and a stable base. Pick it as the middle path between a plain handheld and a full prep station. A small box for the spare blades turns it into a tidy kit, and it is a sensible second slicer even if you already own a larger one.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Gramercy changes thickness with a built-in dial across twelve settings and a rotating cylinder, so you never lift a blade. The Mueller and NACOLUS use interchangeable blades that must be handled and stored. If you prep often, the dial saves time and reduces risk. If you slice once a week, careful swapping is acceptable.

A larger slicer is only safe if it stays put. The Gramercy has a non-slip base with anti-slip feet, while the OXO has a stable foot and bowl hook. Enclosed slicers rely on your pressing hand. Check the base style against your counter surface, and use a damp cloth under any tool that creeps.

The ONCE FOR ALL Plus has a larger feeding port to take chunkier vegetables, while the 4-mode model has a smaller opening. Open platforms like the Gramercy and OXO handle whole potatoes. Think about the biggest vegetable you cut weekly and choose a design that accepts it without pre-cutting.

The Mueller and ONCE FOR ALL Plus both catch food in a container, which keeps counters clear and speeds up prep. Open slicers drop food wherever they sit, so you need a bowl or board. If you cook for a family, a container is a time saver.

More features mean more to store. The Mueller's many blades and the Gramercy's frame need cabinet space. The ONCE FOR ALL Plus collapses for storage, and the OXO and NACOLUS fit in a drawer. Measure before you buy a big station. A tool that cannot find a home in your kitchen will end up unused.

Hidden blades on the ONCE FOR ALL pair, a food holder on the Mueller and a rotating cylinder on the Gramercy each reduce exposure in different ways. Whichever you pick, a cut-resistant glove adds protection during cleaning and blade changes. Wash blades with a brush rather than a sponge pressed toward the edge.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control and settings
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how precisely each pick sets thickness. The Gramercy's twelve-setting dial leads, the OXO's three named thicknesses follow, and enclosed modes on the ONCE FOR ALL rank lower for slice precision but higher for ease.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and prep speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at what fits and how quickly. The Mueller's container and the ONCE FOR ALL Plus's large port favor volume, while the handhelds suit smaller batches.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability
howWeEvaluated.description: Feet, bases and grips counted. The Gramercy's anti-slip feet and the OXO's stable foot scored highest.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety design
howWeEvaluated.description: Hidden blades, rotating cylinders and holders were compared. The ONCE FOR ALL models lead on hidden-edge safety, the Gramercy avoids loose blades, and open handhelds earned less.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and care
howWeEvaluated.description: Parts count and footprint mattered. The OXO and NACOLUS store easily, the Plus model collapses, and the Mueller and Gramercy ask the most of cabinet space.

faq.q: Is the Gramercy worth choosing over a handheld?
faq.a: If you slice often, yes, and the difference shows up most on firm vegetables such as potatoes and beets. Its twelve-setting dial, rotating cylinder and anti-slip feet give better control and steadier results than the OXO. If you slice only occasionally, the handheld saves storage space and costs less to learn.

faq.q: What is odd about the Mueller listing?
faq.a: It describes nine interchangeable blades in the body copy but twelve in the title, so the exact blade count is unclear. Check the contents of the box when it arrives. Count the blades and keep the packing slip until you are satisfied. The food container and holder are the more important features.

faq.q: How does the ONCE FOR ALL Plus differ from the standard model?
faq.a: The Plus has a larger feeding port that takes chunkier vegetables and adds a container, while the standard model has a smaller opening. Both hide the blade and list four mode choices. The Plus also has a collapsible design.

faq.q: Do hidden-blade slicers slice as evenly?
faq.a: Usually not as uniformly as a flat mandoline. The ONCE FOR ALL listing notes less uniformity compared with a flat dial slicer. They are excellent for chopping and quick prep, but critical slices like gratin potatoes may suit the Gramercy better.

faq.q: Do I need a glove with the Gramercy?
faq.a: A cut-resistant glove is a smart addition, since the blade is open and razor sharp. Use the holder, take slow strokes, and keep your fingers away from the final centimeter.

faq.q: Can these dice as well as slice?
faq.a: The Mueller dices with dedicated blades, and the ONCE FOR ALL models list dicing modes. The Gramercy, OXO and NACOLUS focus on slicing, julienne or shredding rather than dicing.
The ONCE FOR ALL Plus collapses so food residue rinses out under the tap. The OXO and NACOLUS are simple shapes. The Gramercy and Mueller have more surfaces, so use a brush and rinse right after use.
